Robert Hanssen was an FBI counterintelligence officer who spied for the Soviet Union and Russia for over twenty years, making him the most damaging mole in FBI history. Arrested in two thousand one, he exposed American intelligence operations and agent identities, rivaling Aldrich Ames in the scope and sensitivity of his betrayals.

Hanssen joined the FBI in nineteen seventy-six and rose through the ranks to become a senior counterintelligence specialist with access to the agency's most sensitive secrets about Soviet and Russian operations. He began spying for the Soviet Union in nineteen seventy-nine, initially motivated by financial hardship and later by ideology and a desire for status. Over his career, he received approximately one point four million dollars in payments.

Working in the FBI's Soviet and Russian counterintelligence section, he gave Moscow advance warning of FBI operations, the names of Russian double agents, and technical surveillance capabilities. His betrayals included compromising the identity of Dmitri Polyakov, a senior KGB officer working as an American spy, who was executed by Moscow. The loss of such assets crippled American intelligence gathering.

Hanssen remained undetected for over twenty years, even after the FBI began investigating a mole in the agency in the nineteen eighties. He was finally caught in two thousand one when a Russian defector provided evidence of his treason. Sentenced to life imprisonment without parole in two thousand two, he remains incarcerated today, having never explained his motivations with clarity or shown remorse.
